text: Dr Sir | Nantes 10th August 1782
I beg leave to Refer to a few lines written by the hand of my Son the
3d Instant, when I was Stretched on my back very Sick, my amanuensis
left me the 8th, he is Returned to Vigan in order to conduct his Sisters
to nantes, from whence We shall all proceed to America as Soon as I
can provide means for that purpose which I hope will be in all
September, You once expressed a wish that I would Return to
England & begin my voyage from thence, nothing would Rejoice
me more, but the Scheme appears impracticable, otherwise I Should
certainly attempt it, Poor as I am, I would give some Guineas
for an hours Conversation with 29, this cant be hoped for, therefore
I must be contented with presenting my dutiful Respects & assurances
of the highest Veneration. But my Dear Sir suppose I Should be
again captured shall I again be dragged to the Tower, Surely this ought
not to be, I have paid value in Exchange for myself, a British
peer [cancelled: ?] Lieutenant General has been Safely delivered in London in
Return for my Enlargement, Ought not I to be indemnify'd untill
I shall Return to my own home too? I think I am fairly
entitled to a Warrantee to extend so far, I beg my friends
will seriously reflect upon this Subject & at least obtain a Letter
from the first Lord of Admiralty or from the Secretaries of State
Recomending me to a benevolent treatment in case I Should meet
with a Second arrest on the Sea, I am persuaded Lord Cornwallis
will if applied to, chearfully assist in obtaining such a Letter
in my favor, it will be but consonant to his Ldsp's voluntary
promises & offers of Service, but if You can do nothing better,
obtain for me a General Letter from one of your friends among
the British Naval Commanders, the Business if it be worth notice
will not admit of delay.
I have not the least objection to your making what Use You please
of my information, Respecting the message Sent to me at Sittingborne
Unless it be to Your asking any body for a Reimbursement of about
four Guineas which the transmission certainly cost me [inserted: x] perhaps five
[cancelled: illegible] [inserted: see below?] Doubt
"You are desired not to communicate any thing of the business
You have been upon to Mr. Bourdieu." [cancelled: ?] Sir it is impossible
"Indeed Sir I was particularly directed to desire you will not communicate any
thing to Mr Bourdieu" — I say Sir it is impossible!
You have here every Syllable that passed & I Know of no other affair
that could have brought the messenger to me, for every thing had been
arranged for my Return to London with only my Servant, the Servant
had been sent to me & was arrived & I was on the point of going
forward when the messenger appeared I paid his whole Expences
to and fro, At least I think so, but an account will prove if
necessary, I am always cautious in assertions, I therefore laid down
my pen & returned to the account & it does not appear that I paid the
Expence, this serves however to demonstrate, the Message was Special
& not on my account for I paid all other Expences of the Journey.
I have at length written to 21 on Your affair, I say at length
because our interchanges have not been very quick, tho the 19
has been abundantly polite & I may say friendly, what I have said
will be communicated to 55 or 57. "68 is a great Stickler for 36,
& I [cancelled: ?] believe a faithful friend to his own Country, but 54 is pleased
to think him much too much in the Interest of 23. & has treated
him [inserted: in my opinion] as a Bystander in a very unwarrantable manner." "
I fancy the Business must be now obsolete & I dare venture to say
neither 56 nor 19 have heard [cancelled: nor] thought of any thing to
the dishonour or prejudice of 67. Be that as it may You
shall be informed of all I may Collect from 20.
I thank You most Sincerely for Your Repeated assurances
of attachment, but when I hinted a Revolution of trading
upon my own Stock I was on a Political carpet & had no
Ideas of per Centums in my head; it is in all appearance too late
in the day for me to think of Commerce, You cannot conceive
how hardly I have labored to get on so far & so clumsily with
this Short address. I have been at least three hours upon it
which formerly I would have dispatched in less than ½ of an
hour; Long Confinement has shiver'd one of the Best Constitutions
in the world, but under all difficulties Reverse of fortune & a
desire of providing for my children may oblige me even to go [cancelled: ?]
into trade again [cancelled: ?] before I have [inserted?] after I
shall have rendered an account to my Constituents but not before;
in such Extremity You will hear from me.
I am totally ignorant of what is going forward in the Diplomatick
Group at Paris, Can You inform me & say, what is the Cause,
amidst Your Successes in the East & in the West, of the fall of
Stocks? How sits the Check which Lord G's messengers received
from an uncourtly Congress upon the minds of Your people, or
do they think lightly of that which will render St James's
the Jest of every Court in Europe & the Contempt of America.
His Ldp. vainly imagined he had an influence upon the
people of America which they know nothing of, Yes he
said to me. "the Constitution of Great Britain is Sufficient
to pervade the whole world" I endeavoured to persuade [cancelled: ?] his
Ldp. to take things as they were, I assured him if he was in
earnest in the work of peace it must be accomplish'd at his own
door & put into his hands the Copy of a Commission appointing
persons to be treated with but he chose to feel pulses again
at 1000 Leagues distance & never entertained one forethought
of the awkwardness of attempting to wheedle a people after
Seven Years ineffectual efforts to beat them into Compliance.
Aye? but surely they will be content to be upon the same
footing with Ireland; Surely not, the Respective cases differ widely,
You have driven America to Extremities & [inserted: have] learned from Consequences
to deal with more temporizing [inserted: policy] the work of necessity, toward
Ireland, Such tamperings as we have lately seen will be
of more real Service to the American Cause than another
York Town Surrender. I have the honour to be
with sincere Esteem & regard
Sir Yr obliged & obed Servt.
James Bourdieu Esq.
London
